sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do the main image and the headline make one idea together, with neither just repeating the other?** No.
   - **Where:** The headline "Savings deposits rose every month" (48–590, y≈145) only says in words what the six rising bars already show. The chart's loudest feature is June: $1150k (721–783, y≈312–637), a jump of about a third on May's $868k when every earlier month rose by $40–80k. The headline doesn't mention it.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** They read June as a surge in member saving. The reason, "June includes the mid-year bonus payroll", appears only in the small grey source line at y≈717, below the chart card, where most readers won't look. The $4.82M total and its "Up 6.1%" carry the same one-off without saying so.
   - **Why:** The headline and the chart should make one claim together. Here the headline repeats the trend and leaves the outlier unexplained, so the piece's biggest number tells a different story from the one the maker knows is true. This is common sense; the catalog entry, "Visual and headline work together", has no approved source.
   - **Fix:** Name the cause where the eye already is. Put it in the dek, such as "…June includes the mid-year bonus payroll", or as a direct note at the June bar. Then the steady rise and the one-off June bump read as two distinct facts.
   - Defect, because it invites a wrong reading of the largest figure. Weight: major.
2. **Does every element, rule, box, and ornament do a job, so that removing it would lose something?** No.
   - **Where:** The chart title "Deposits into savings accounts, US dollars per month" (68, y≈250) restates the subtitle "New money paid into member savings accounts, by month, January to June 2026" (48, y≈185), about 65 px above.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** They read the same description twice. The only new information in the chart title is the unit.
   - **Fix:** Fold the unit into the subtitle and drop or shorten the chart title, or keep the chart title and cut the subtitle down to what the chart doesn't say.
   - Taste (common sense). Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- **One coherent voice.** The logo and headline share a sturdy serif, everything else is a quiet sans, and the palette is one blue plus green for the "Up…" lines. That reads as calm, credible and institutional, which suits a credit union reporting to its members.
- **The numbers agree with each other.** The six bars sum to the $4.82M total, and 5,374 accounts × $214 average ≈ $1.15M, which matches the June bar. Every figure on the page supports one story, which builds trust in a report.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 6 yes, 2 no (main image and headline make one idea; every element does a job), 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** What matters first (hierarchy): applies.

**Findings**
None.

All three lines come out yes after reading the entries. One thing for the director to weigh: the three KPI figures on the right ($4.82M at about 880–1030 × 262–298, $214, 5,374) look about as large as the headline, around 32 px bold, so the right column is a close second stop for the eye. They don't fail the "distinct levels" line. Their sans form, smaller width and place in the cards keep them clearly a level below the serif headline, and the "Sizes come from a scale" entry is about near-matching body text, which this isn't. If the director wants a clearer lead for the headline, setting the KPI figures one step smaller would be a taste call, not a defect.

**What's working.**
- **A clear order down the page.** The serif bold headline at the top left (48–590 × 128–162) is the one place the eye starts. It is the only serif text on the page apart from the logo, so it reads as the title by its form as well as its size. A small uppercase label sits above it and a plain grey summary line below it, which sets up a clean three-step order before the chart. Keep the serif for the headline only.
- **The small text stays sorted.** The KPI labels are grey, the values heavy and black, and the change lines green. The chart title is bold and the axis and source text are small and grey. Several small sizes sit close together, but colour and weight tell them apart, not size. That is the right way to do it (Refactoring UI: bolder, not bigger; lighter, not smaller).

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

I've checked the reference entries and am writing the report now.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: this section applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do all blocks take their edges and gaps from one grid, so gutters repeat down the page?** No. The two columns sit 32 px apart (chart card ends at x≈848, KPI cards start at x≈880). The three KPI cards stacked on the right are only about 17 px apart (y≈340–357 and 479–496). The page doesn't stick to one spacing value, so the right column looks tighter and slightly squeezed next to the chart. The fix is to use one spacing value, probably the 32 px column gutter, for the gaps between the KPI cards too. (Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*: grid fields are separated by one fixed interval.) Convention. Weight: minor.
2. **Is every element exactly aligned or clearly off, with no near-misses?** and **Do lines of text in neighboring columns sit on the same baselines?** Both no, one defect. The chart title "Deposits into savings accounts, US dollars per month" sits at about y≈250. The first KPI label "Total deposited, Jan to Jun 2026" sits at about y≈246. The two card tops line up at y≈218, so these first lines are clearly meant to line up and miss by about 4 px. The top row looks a little unfinished. The fix is to give the chart card and the KPI cards the same top padding and line height so the first lines share a baseline. (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance": a placement that is almost aligned makes the eye waver. Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems*: neighbouring columns share baselines.) Convention. Weight: minor. Measure in a live browser to confirm the exact offset.
3. **Is the empty space gathered into a few deliberate areas, rather than left over in scattered small gaps?** No. The KPI stack ends at y≈618 and the chart card ends at y≈693, which leaves a 75 px gap at the bottom right. The gap isn't small enough to look aligned or big enough to look deliberate. Below the source line there is also a loose empty band (y≈730–800). The bottom of the layout looks ragged rather than finished. The fix is to make the two columns end on the same line. You can stretch the three cards, or use the gutter fix in finding 1 to spread them over the chart's height. Alternatively, make the KPI column clearly shorter on purpose. (Ruder, *Typography: A Manual of Design*: empty space should be gathered, not left over.) Taste, building on that convention. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- Everything shares one strong left edge at x=48: the logo, eyebrow, headline, subtitle, chart card and source line. The right edge mirrors it with a 48 px margin at x≈1232. The page reads as one ordered column without effort.
- The layout is a wide chart with a narrow stack of KPI cards beside it, with the chart taking about 70% of the width. The main evidence gets the most room, the summary numbers sit right beside it, and the eye moves cleanly from headline to bars to totals.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 9 yes, 4 no (one grid with repeating gutters; exact alignment with no near-misses; baselines across columns; white space gathered).

I've finished the checklist walk and checked the borderline contrast line. Here is the report.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**

No checklist line in this section ends as `no`.

One note on the copy, which no checklist line covers: the green comparison lines in the three cards, "Up 6.1% on Jan to Jun 2025" (≈900,313), "Up $11 on Jun 2025" (≈900,452) and "Up 402 on Jun 2025" (≈900,591), cut the words that say what is being compared. "Up $11 on Jun 2025" could mean "compared with June 2025" or "something that happened in June 2025". Most readers will guess right, but they still have to work it out. The fix is to name the comparison, for example "Up $11 on June 2025" → "$11 more than in June 2025", or "Up 6.1% on the same months of 2025". This is taste (common sense); it's minor.

**What's working.**
- **The typeface plan is clear.** A bold serif is used only for the wordmark and the headline. A plain sans carries everything else: deck, chart title, labels, card text and source line. The two faces are plainly different, so the headline reads as the voice of the page and nothing else competes with it.
- **The small text is set with care.** The all-caps eyebrow "MEMBER REPORT, FIRST HALF 2026" (≈48,105) is letterspaced. The deck runs about 75 characters on one flush-left line. Axis labels, bar labels and the source line are small but stay at a readable weight and size, and none is clipped.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**

The mid-grey source line at the bottom (≈48,717) sits on the light grey page tint (around #f6f7f9), not on white, as do the grey card labels. Both look readable, but if the grey is close to #6b7280 the ratio would be about 4.4–4.6:1, right at the 4.5:1 line (WCAG 1.4.3). It's worth measuring the source line against the page tint in a browser.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

sections.report:
**Section.** Charts and data: applies (one monthly bar chart and three figure cards on a credit union's member report).

**Findings**
1. **Does a title or caption state the chart's finding in words?** The headline "Savings deposits rose every month" (48,130–590,160) states a finding, and it is true. But the June bar (721–783, top ≈312) is the tallest mark by far at $1150k, a jump of $282k when earlier months rose by $43k to $79k. The only explanation, "June includes the mid-year bonus payroll", is the last clause of a small grey source line at y≈717, under the chart card. A member sees the June spike first and reads it as savings speeding up. Most will never connect it to the footnote. The June figure also feeds the $4.82M total and the June-only cards ($214 average, 5,374 accounts), which are all lifted by the bonus. Without an approved source this is common sense: the most striking mark has a one-off cause, so that cause belongs on the mark. Fix: put a short note at the June bar ("includes mid-year bonus payroll"), or split June into regular and bonus parts with the bonus in a lighter tint. Then check that the headline still holds without the bonus. Defect. Weight: major.
2. **Does each chart show enough of the time range or sample to judge the trend?** The chart shows January to June 2026 only. The first card says the half-year total is up only 6.1% on 2025, so 2025 probably rose through the same months. If so, "rose every month" is partly seasonal, and nothing on the chart lets the viewer tell. Six months is the report's natural period, not cherry-picked, so this is a smaller point. Fix: add the same months of 2025 as a pale grey reference (ghost bars or a thin line), so the rise is judged against last year. The approved list has no source for this, so it is my judgment. Taste. Weight: minor.
3. **Do the labels in each chart stay clear of each other and of the marks?** The "$1150k" value label (≈731–775, y≈297) sits right on the $1200k gridline and level with the "$1200k" axis label, so the line runs through or touches the text. The catalog has no entry for this, so it is common sense. Fix: raise the top of the scale a little, or drop the top gridline, so the label has clear space above the bar. Defect. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The scale is honest and the labels are complete. Bars start at $0k, ticks step evenly by $300k, the chart title gives the unit ("US dollars per month"), every bar has its value, and the source line gives the ledger and cut-off date. The figures add up: the six bars sum to the $4.82M card, and $214 × 5,374 ≈ $1.15M matches June. A member can trust the arithmetic.
- Each figure card carries a period and a comparison with last year ("Up 6.1% on Jan to Jun 2025", "Up 402 on Jun 2025"), so no big number stands alone (Few, "Common Pitfalls in Dashboard Design", pitfall 2).

**Checklist.** Charts and data: 16 lines, 13 yes, 3 no (title or caption states the finding; enough time range; labels clear of each other and the marks)

sections.report:
**Section.** Interface: applies. The only controls are the four text links in the top nav. There are no buttons, fields, dialogs or interactive chart controls.

**Findings**
1. **Do the navigation and components follow the conventions users know from the platform and similar products?** The header of a credit union site (y≈0–63) has the wordmark and four links (Accounts, Member report, Rates, Branches, x≈372–739). There is no sign-in or online banking entry, and the right half of the bar (x≈740–1280) is empty. A member who lands here from a newsletter and wants to check their own savings will look top-right for "Log in", the usual place on banking sites. They won't find it, and may click "Accounts" hoping it gets them there. Jakob's law (Nielsen, *End of Web Design* / NN/g) says to use the pattern users already know unless breaking it gains something, and nothing is gained here. The fix: put a sign-in link or a small secondary button at the right end of the nav. If "Accounts" means account products, rename it ("Savings & checking", "Open an account") so it isn't mistaken for "my accounts". This is a convention. It doesn't affect the page's job, which is reporting deposit growth, but it costs members who want to act on what they just read. Weight: minor.

**What's working.** The current page is marked twice. "Member report" in the nav is bold and dark navy against grey neighbours, and the eyebrow "MEMBER REPORT, FIRST HALF 2026" (y≈105) repeats it above the headline, so it's clear where you are without relying on colour alone. The nav is also short, in plain member language ("Rates", "Branches"), at the top-left where people expect it, and nothing fixed or pop-up covers the content.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the nav links show a visible focus indicator (at least 2 px thick, 3:1 contrast) and a hover state.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 31 yes, 1 no (navigation follows known conventions), 1 unsure (focus indicator)
